Investors are betting on more upside in US Treasuries.

The extra cost investors are willing to pay for call options on longer-dated Treasuries relative to puts is up to ~50 basis points, the highest since March 2025.

This marks a sharp reversal from a 250-basis-point premium for puts over calls in late September.

This suggests investors are increasingly betting on further gains in Treasury prices.

Furthermore, one options trade is targeting a drop in the 10Y Note Yield to ~4.60% within a month, involving ~65,000 contracts and costing ~$7 million in premium.

This comes as the 10Y Note Yield has declined below 5.00% for the first time since September 23rd, now down -40 basis points from the October 7th peak.

The bond market is seeing massive swings in price and sentiment.

Of course, I can’t let a WAAR go by without one of my excel-crashing 3D scatterplots. This one shows the spread between the real yield and potential real GDP growth (x-axis) against the 5yr CAPE ratio in the y-axis. The size of the dots shows the 12m real return for the S&P 500. There are clearly two tails here, both bad, while the middle of the curve is the sweet spot. Note that we are kind of “out there” right now in terms of how positive the real yield is vs the growth rate and how high valuations against that backdrop. The 1987 crash, the GFC, and the 1994 Greenspan rate cycle all happened on the right side of this bell curve, while the dot. com bubble was close to where we are now, and the 2021 mini bubble was to the left.

The US government cannot afford higher interest rates.

If interest rates average +150 basis points above CBO’s February projections by 2036, US deficits would increase by nearly $6 trillion over this period.

The deficit would then rise to 8.8% of GDP, the highest level since WWII, excluding 2008 and 2020.

This would also push the US public Debt-to-GDP ratio to a record 133%, up from ~100% currently.

If rates average +50 basis points above projections, deficits would increase by nearly $2 trillion, lifting the Debt-to-GDP ratio to 124% by 2036.

Just weeks ago, the 10Y Note yield traded at ~5.30%, or ~100 basis points above CBO’s average projected rate over the next 10 years.

The US government needs rate cuts.

With bond yields coming off the boil last week, perhaps we are now settling into a range for a bit. While the CPI came in hotter than expected, there is currently little pressure on the Fed to raise rates at the end of October. While the consensus appears to be that yields have moved higher because of strong economic growth, and that they are now moving a bit lower because of a possible slowdown in AI capex, in my view the rise in yields this year has been multi-factorial, including sticky structural inflation and mounting fiscal risk.

On the valuation side, the forward P/E-multiple is now 19x and the 5-year CAPE ratio is at 27x. That’s very high but it includes 2021, which was just on the heels of the COVID crash. In an attempt to make the CAPE ratio less backward-looking, I adjusted it by using consensus next 18-month estimates instead a pure 5-year lookback. That brings the CAPE ratio down from 33x to 27x. That’s still high but considerably lower than where the operating margin suggests it should be. If the earnings boom continues, the CAPE ratio will likely come down as the newer higher estimates come in and the older lower numbers roll off.

BREAKING: China purchased +25 tonnes of gold in August via the London OTC market, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.

This is +25% more than the official +20 tonnes reported by China's central bank for this month.

This also follows estimated purchases of +35, +40, and +48 tonnes in July, June, and May, respectively.

Over these 4 months, China's estimated gold purchases through the OTC market exceeded officially reported purchases by 83 tonnes, or +128%.

Meanwhile, global central banks are estimated to have acquired +79 tonnes of gold in August, +365% above the pre-2022 average of +17 tonnes.

China is stockpiling gold.
